threads_text: Delaware is drafting a law for companies run day to day by an AI agent, and the House Oversight Committee just demanded every document behind it by November 9. Supporters say AI-run businesses are coming anyway. Would you sign a contract with a company that has no human boss?
caption:
Delaware is drafting a law for a new kind of business, the Artificial Intelligence Company, run day to day by an AI agent.
House Oversight chair James Comer has asked Gov. Matt Meyer for the documents behind it, including internal AI chat logs, by November 9.
State lawmakers are expected to take up the bill in January 2027.

Would you trust a company with no human in charge?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: WHYY, House Oversight Committee · Photos: Emma Lee/WHYY

slides.headline: Delaware wants to let *AI agents run entire companies*. Congress just demanded answers

slides.heading: A company with *no human boss*
paras: A draft Delaware law would create the "Artificial Intelligence Company," with an AI agent running its day-to-day business.
It could own property, sign contracts and sue or be sued. Banking is off-limits.

slides.heading: Who pays when *the AI messes up*?
paras: One person or company must keep it funded, and is shielded from its debts unless it underfunds it or uses it for fraud.

paras.t: The AI agent must keep a log of everything it does.

slides.heading: Congress *wants the receipts*
paras: On October 26, House Oversight chair James Comer asked Gov. Matt Meyer for records back to January 2025, including internal AI chat logs.
He warned the plan could shield AI companies from responsibility for harm.
slides.note: Delaware has until November 9 to answer.

slides.heading: What happens *next*
paras: Meyer's office says it is reviewing the letter. State lawmakers are expected to take up the bill in January 2027.
If it passes, AI companies would be tested in a 30-month regulatory sandbox.

slides.hook: The first company run by an AI could be registered in Delaware. Follow to see if it happens.

site_article.headline: House Oversight Committee questions Delaware plan for companies run by AI agents

site_article.summary: The House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform has asked Delaware for documents on its proposal to let AI agents run companies day to day. Chairman James Comer set a November 9, 2026 deadline.
site_article.seo_title: Congress questions Delaware's plan for AI-run companies
site_article.seo_description: House Oversight chair James Comer asked Delaware for records on its proposed AI-run company law, including internal AI chat logs, by November 9.
site_article.answer_summary: Delaware is drafting a law for an Artificial Intelligence Company run day to day by an AI agent. On October 26, 2026, House Oversight chair James Comer asked the state for its records on the plan by November 9.
site_article.hero_alt: A humanoid robot in a suit signing papers alone at the head of a long boardroom table.

paragraphs.text: The House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform has asked Delaware for records on its proposal to create companies run day to day by AI agents. In a letter dated October 26, 2026, Chairman James Comer, a Kentucky Republican, asked Gov. Matt Meyer to turn over documents about the proposed Artificial Intelligence Company, or AIC, by November 9.

Comer wrote that the framework could protect powerful AI companies and their investors from responsibility for harmful conduct, according to the letter and WHYY's reporting. He also raised concerns about regulatory capture, in which hidden interests could use state rules to block competitors, and said the process behind the proposal did not appear transparent.

The letter requests documents and communications about the AIC dating back to January 1, 2025, including exchanges with outside parties and internal AI chat logs. It also asks for ethics and consulting agreements with outside contributors, records of anyone consulted about safety concerns and potential harms, and all drafts and comments on the proposal. Ranking Member Robert Garcia was copied on the letter.

A deputy press secretary for Meyer said the governor's office is reviewing the letter, WHYY reported. Norm Ai founder and CEO John Nay, whose company is working with the state on the framework, did not respond to WHYY's request for comment.

Delaware Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez and Nay announced the plan in a Fortune commentary in July 2026 as a public-private partnership. Under the draft, an AIC could hold property, take on obligations and sue or be sued in its own name, with an AI agent directing its daily operations. It could pursue any lawful purpose except banking.

Each AIC would need a single human or corporate member who must keep it adequately funded, and the AI agent would have to log its activity. The member would be shielded from the company's debts unless it failed to capitalize the company or used it for fraud or a willful violation of law. Companies would operate inside a regulatory sandbox, with a 30-month window to apply after the law takes effect, overseen by a committee that includes the Secretary of State, the Attorney General and the chief justice of the state Supreme Court.

The letter names John Mark Zeberkiewicz, a lawyer at Richards, Layton & Finger, as the principal drafter of a 36-page draft released in late June 2026. State lawmakers are expected to consider the bill in January 2027, according to Startup Fortune. Legal scholars quoted by WHYY were divided, with one warning there is no overall plan for the fallout and another arguing that Delaware would be irresponsible to ignore the issue.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the dispute is less about whether AI agents will run business tasks and more about who is liable when they cause harm. Delaware's long lead in forming companies and LLCs gives any new entity type created there unusual reach, which helps explain why a state proposal has drawn federal attention before it has even reached a vote.
The next marker is November 9, when Delaware's response to the committee's document request is due.
